Khong Wong Yai 用於泰國音樂，尤其皮帕特合奏，為合奏中其他樂器提供: The Khong Wong Yai is used in Thai music, especially in the piphat ensemble, where it supplies the skeletal melody on which the other instruments build; the source also mentions that it is an important instrument of Thai music bands and orchestras. It sounds as an idiophone: sixteen tuned bossed gongs are set in a circle, the player sits in the middle, and strikes them with soft or hard beaters. In Cambodian music its counterpart is the Kong Thom.

大鑼圈在泰國音樂中具悠久歷史，自古為重要樂器，也是泰國樂隊與皮帕特合奏的主要樂器: The Khong Wong Yai has a long history in Thai music, has been an important instrument since ancient times, and is a principal instrument of Thai bands and the piphat ensemble. Its origin is connected with drums, and the early evidence points to the area around Yunnan in southern China; it later spread to Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Related objects use the same alloy as today's gongs, and the form gradually developed into a disc closer to a gong. The kang sadan found at Wat Haripunchai in Lamphun is a large disc about 2 metres across, dated to around the thirteenth century, which shows the line of development. In Cambodian music it corresponds to the kong thom.
大鑼圈由十六面凸鈕鑼排成圓圈，每面以中心凸鈕發出一個主要音，聲音來自鑼體自身振動: The Khong Wong Yai sets sixteen bossed gongs in a circle, and each gong gives one main note from its central boss, the sound coming from the vibration of the gong itself. The pitches are arranged from low to high, the highest being the sixteenth gong; the source records reference pitches of 378 hertz and 760 hertz, and pitch is adjusted by sticking a mixture of wax and lead under the gong, less lead giving a higher pitch and more lead a lower one. The source is not clear on how volume is controlled, recording only that soft or hard beaters may be used. Acoustic analysis shows beating between paired notes at six to twelve per second, and for higher pairs a roughness at eighteen to forty-two per second, along with non-harmonic overtones. It serves the same function as the Cambodian kong thom, providing the skeletal melody in the piphat ensemble.
大鑼圈的鑼圈以藤製成，並附著桃花心木；支撐件用木料、竹與金屬線，另有玻璃珠。發聲: The gong circle of the Khong Wong Yai is made of rattan with mahogany attached; the supports use wood, bamboo and wire, and there are glass beads as well. The sixteen bossed gongs that sound were once bronze and are mostly brass today, formed by hot forging or casting. They are tuned underneath with beeswax and lead, less lead giving a higher pitch and more lead a lower one. It is played with hard rubber or soft-padded beaters.
大鑼圈（Khong Wong Yai）是泰國音樂中的體鳴樂器，由十六面調音凸心鑼: The Khong Wong Yai is an idiophone of Thai music: sixteen tuned bossed gongs are set in a circle on a rattan frame. The player sits in the middle of the circle and strikes with two beaters, soft or hard; the pitch of each gong is adjusted with beeswax underneath. In the Thai piphat ensemble it supplies the skeletal melody on which the other instruments unfold.

演奏者坐於大鑼圈中央，可盤腿或交腿，雙手各持一槌，以中指、無名指與小指收攏，拇指: The player sits in the middle of the Khong Wong Yai, cross-legged or with the legs folded to one side, a beater in each hand, held with the middle, ring and little fingers closed and the thumb and index finger supporting it, the index finger near the head. The gong is struck on the raised centre of its face, with a soft or a hard beater. A beginner first masters the division of labour between the hands: when the melody has two notes at once, the right hand plays the higher and the left the lower, and the same for fourths or octaves. Runs of sixteenth notes can be played by alternating the hands symmetrically, adjusting the position of the hands to the shape of the melody.
